lesson.title: One Mind, Many Tasks: Spearman and the Case for General Intelligence
lesson.summary: Spearman's discovery that scores on different mental tests tend to correlate led him to propose g, a general intelligence factor underlying performance across cognitive tasks.
lesson.body:
When psychologists in the early twentieth century began giving people batteries of different mental tests, ranging from vocabulary to arithmetic to spatial puzzles, they noticed something curious: people who scored well on one type of test tended to score well on nearly all the others, even tasks that seemed to have little in common on the surface. This pattern, often called the positive manifold, was the empirical starting point for one of the most influential and debated ideas in the history of testing, the idea of a single general intelligence factor, usually labeled g.

The English psychologist Charles Spearman formalized this idea in 1904 using a statistical technique he helped develop called factor analysis, a method for identifying whether correlations among many different measurements can be explained by a smaller number of underlying factors. Applying this method to test scores, Spearman proposed a two factor theory of intelligence: performance on any given task reflects a contribution from g, the general factor shared across all cognitive tasks, plus a contribution from s, a factor specific to that particular task or skill. On this view, a strong vocabulary and strong mental math ability tend to travel together not because one causes the other, but because both draw partly on the same underlying general capacity.

This is a good example of psychology as a science in action, since Spearman's claim was not just a philosophical assertion but a testable statistical model built from real correlational data, and it has been tested, extended, and challenged by generations of researchers using that same scientific method. Later psychologists proposed competing or complementary structures. Louis Thurstone argued in the 1930s that intelligence was better described by several relatively independent primary mental abilities rather than one dominant factor. Raymond Cattell and John Horn later distinguished fluid intelligence, the ability to reason and solve novel problems, from crystallized intelligence, the accumulated knowledge and skills a person has built over a lifetime, both of which still correlate with each other and with broader measures of g.

What g actually represents is still debated. Some researchers treat it as evidence of a real, measurable general cognitive capacity, possibly tied to processing speed or working memory efficiency in the brain. Others argue that g is at least partly a statistical artifact of how test batteries are constructed, or that it reflects shared exposure to schooling, language, and test taking conventions rather than one unified brain capacity. What is not seriously disputed is the underlying data pattern itself: across a wide range of standardized cognitive tests, scores tend to correlate positively with one another, and this positive manifold is the empirical foundation that every later theory of intelligence, including the more specific and educational approach covered in the next chapter, has had to explain or challenge.
